newsitem.title: UK: Ferocious UK petrol market shows it still has bite.
newsitem.headline: Ferocious UK petrol market shows it still has bite.

text.p: Britain's petrol margins narrowed in the last six weeks and the price-setting supermarkets signalled renewed aggressiveness that could squeeze profits for independent retailers, analysts said.
Oil companies expressed relief at the recovery in margins at the end of 1996 from the roughly two pence per litre nadir that was touched at the height of the price war last summer.

But at four to five pence per litre they are seen as below break-even for some independent filling stations, who are still reeling from an industry shakeout last year that was sparked by Esso's Pricewatch.
An unexpected result from Pricewatch has been greater price differentials where the oil companies are not competing head-to-head with the supermarkets, such as in rural areas, analysts said.
Esso, a unit of U.S. oil giant Exxon, launched its Pricewatch campaign a year ago promising to match its lowest-priced competitors.
"With margins at these levels, it's definitely going to squeeze the market," said Andrew Bradley, senior consultant at Wood Mackenzie in Edinburgh.
"It's indicative of the supermarkets willing to keep margins where they can make a profit and assert some control over the market," he said.

Retail margins for unleaded petrol in the U.K. narrowed to 4.7 pence per litre for major brand operators in mid-February, down from five pence in January and 5.3 pence in December, according to Oil Price Assessments Ltd (OPAL).
Auto diesel margins recovered slightly in February to five pence per litre from 4.6 pence in December, as spot gas oil prices fell quicker than those at the pump.

"The supermarkets seem to be quite aggressive at the moment," said Peter Regnier, director of OPAL. Regarding margins, he said, "Yes, it is better than the extreme of the price war but it still isn't glorious."
"We don't expect margins to recover to pre-Pricewatch levels pence per litre because now the supermarkets are the price setters," Bradley said.
"Because of the inherent cost structure the supermarkets can turn a profit on margins of 4-5 pence per litre," where margins are likely to stay, he said.
He said margins recovered slightly at the end of 1996 because Shell temporarily led the market higher, and not due to fewer filling stations.
"This year is not going to be as profitable as pre-Pricewatch but it could turn out to be better than 1996," he said.
Shell Chairman John Jennings, without quantifying the impact on earnings last year, told a press briefing last week that margins were still not acceptable.
"The margins appeared to have recovered a bit but are still not sufficient to provide a return on our downstream investment in the U.K. that would be considered satisfactory," he said.
British Petroleum said last week that the price war cost it $140 million in 1996 but that margins were finding a degree of equilibrium and were now profitable.
